'''''Acacia auriculiformis''''', commonly known as '''ear-pod wattle''', '''northern black wattle''' or '''Darwin black wattle''',<ref name="FoA">{{cite web |last1=Kodela |first1=Phillip G. |last2=Maslin |first2=Bruce R. |editor-last1=Kodela |editor-first1=Phillip G. |title=''Acacia auriculiformis'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Acacia%20auriculiformis |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water: Canberra. |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref><ref name="NT">{{cite web |title=''Acacia auriculiformis'' |url=https://eflora.nt.gov.au/factsheet?id=3401 |publisher=Northern Territory Government |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref><ref name="DES">{{cite web |title=Species profile—''Acacia auriculiformis'' |url=https://apps.des.qld.gov.au/species-search/details/?id=15828 |publisher=Queensland Government, Department of Education and Science |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Fabaceae]] and is [[Native species|native]] to [[Maluku Islands|Maluku]], [[New Guinea]], the [[Northern Territory]] and [[Queensland]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Acacia auriculiformis'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:469784-1 |publisher=Plants of the World Online |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref> It is a tree with smooth bark, very narrowly elliptic [[phyllode]]s, spikes of bright yellow to golden-yellow flowers, and strongly curved to spirally coiled, leathery to woody [[Pod (fruit)|pods]] up to {{cvt|80|mm}} long.

==Description==
''Acacia auriculiformis'' is a tree that typically grows to {{cvt|8–10|m}} high, rarely up to {{cvt|35|m}}, and is mostly [[wikt:glabrous|glabrous]], with smooth bark or fissured bark on older trees, and thin branchlets. The phyllodes are very narrowly elliptic, sometimes curved, mostly {{cvt|100–200|mm}} long and {{cvt|12–40|mm}} wide with many longitudinal veins, three to five more prominent than the rest. The flowers are bright yellow to golden-yellow, arranged in one to several spikes in leaf axils, each spike {{cvt|50–85|mm}} long on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|4–8|mm}} long. Flowering occurs from February to August, and the fruit is a strongly curved or spirally coiled, sometimes twisted, thickly leathery to woody pod about {{cvt|50–80|mm}} long and {{cvt|10–18|mm}} wide, containing flattened, dark brown to black seeds {{cvt|4–6|mm}} long and {{cvt|3–4|mm}} wide with an orange, yellow or red [[aril]].<ref name="FoA" /><ref name="NT" /><ref name="www">{{cite web |title=''Acacia auriculiformis'' |url=https://worldwidewattle.com/speciesgallery/auriculiformis.php |publisher=World Wide Wattle |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Acacia auriculiformis'' was first formally described in 1842 by [[George Bentham]] in [[William Jackson Hooker|Hooker's]] ''London Journal of Botany'', from an unpublished description by [[Allan Cunningham (botanist)|Allan Cunningham]].<ref name="APNI">{{cite web |title=''Acacia auriculiformis'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/463139 |publisher=Australian Plant Name Index |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref><ref name="Benth.">{{cite journal |last1=Bentham |first1=George |title=Notes on Mimoseae, with a synopsis of species. |journal=London Journal of Botany |date=1842 |volume=1 |page=377 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/40367#page/381/mode/1up |access-date=14 February 2025}}</ref> The [[specific epithet]] (''auriculiformis'') means 'ear shaped', referring to the pods.<ref name="FoA" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Ear-pod wattle grows in sandy or loamy soils near watercourses and swamps in open forest on [[Cape York Peninsula]] in Queensland, the north of the Northern Territory, the [[Central Province (Papua New Guinea)|Central]] and [[Western Province (Papua New Guinea)|Western Provinces]] of New Guinea, and the [[Kai Islands|Kei Islands]] of Indonesia. It is also recorded as [[naturalised]] in Western Australia.<ref name="FoA" /><ref name="NT" /><ref name="www" />

== Uses ==
Extracts of ''Acacia auriculiformis'' [[heartwood]] inhibit fungi that attack wood.<ref>[http://www.arkat-usa.org/Arkivoc/Journal content/manuscripts/2007/UR-2002CR%20as%20published%20mainmanuscript.pdf Active antifungal substances from natural sources]</ref> Aqueous extracts of ''A. auriculiformis'' show developmental inhibitory effects on ''[[Bactrocera cucurbitae]]'' (the melon fly).<ref name="JoB">{{cite journal |last1=Kaur |first1=Amandeep |last2=Sohal |first2=S.K. |last3=Singh |first3=Rajbir |last4=Arora |first4=Saroj |title=Development inhibitory effect of ''Acacia auriculiformis'' extracts on ''Bactrocera cucurbitae'' (Coquillett) (Diptera:Tephritidae) |journal=Journal of Biopesticides |date=2010 |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=499–504 |url=https://jbiopestic.com/journals/Amandeep_Kaur_V32.pdf |access-date=15 February 2025}}</ref>
